text.p: Venezuela virtually ground to a halt on Wednesday as unions unleashed their first general strike in eight years, a crippling 12-hour stoppage over pay that the government said was justified.

The Venezuelan Workers Confederation (CTV), the country's largest union, staged the walkout to protest against the private sector's failure to make promised wage rises. It said the strike was a success and participation was massive.
"At least 90 percent of the workforce joined the strike," CTV President Federico Ramirez Leon told reporters.
"Today's civic protest showed foreign investors that Venezuela is a reliable country for them," he added, stressing that "in many countries days like this end with pitched battles."
The leading business chamber, Fedecamaras, agreed the strike had a major nationwide impact, but only because most Venezuelans could not find public transport to go to work.
Government offices were shut and public transport was non-existent in Venezuela's main cities, forcing employees and workers to stay home, radio reports said.
Telephone and electric services were unaffected, banks and financial markets remained open and airport officials said domestic and international flights operated normally.
State oil giant Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), which controls the largest oil reserves outside the Middle East, said it continued normal operations thanks to a contingency plan.
Caracas streets were quieter than usual with armed police and National Guardsmen stationed at key installations. No incidents were reported and there were no protest marches.
The Caracas Stock Exchange closed up 1.84 percent with a cautious market apparently confident the peaceful stoppage would have no lingering ill effects on the economy.

The stoppage -- the fifth general strike in Venezuela since the country's return to democracy in 1958 -- won the unusual backing of the government of President Rafael Caldera and broad support from across the political spectrum.
Outspoken Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff, who fought a communist guerrilla movement against the government in the 1960s, reiterated on Wednesday the strike was "justified".
"The unionized sector must fight for its rights ... this is an alarm bell for the business sector," he told reporters.

Union and government officials lambasted business leaders for failing to raise wages as agreed in a March deal to reform the complex social security system. But some business leaders ridiculed the government's "lack of seriousness" in endorsing the strike, which was also called to protest against last week's 27 percent hike in gasoline prices.
Fedecamaras head Francisco Natera said the strike "only aggravates deep-rooted problems, inflation, unemployment, corruption, resulting in domestic and foreign investors' loss of confidence."
CTV's Ramirez Leon replied "there is nothing worse than a blind man who doesn't want to see."
Business chamber leaders say 90 percent of their members have increased pay in accordance with the March deal.

A commission made up of government, business and union representatives was set up last week to investigate whether the wage hikes had been awarded. They will meet again on Thursday and Notera pledged to seek a just solution "through dialogue."
With Venezuela still groggy after three years of recession, runaway inflation and delayed salary rises have reduced real wages to one-third of their 1960s level, according to official figures.
